Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Places of worship or religious gatherings

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette:
Leilani was thirty-nine when she finally walked into a therapist’s office, nearly four years after she came home from the war zone. Before that, she had been a relief worker in a besieged city—seventy-two days of shelling, shortages, and the constant calculus of who to help first. She remembered the scent of a specific cologne that a dying man wore as she held his hand, unable to do more. She remembered the way a colleague had hugged her afterward, a gesture meant to comfort, but that touch now carried a violation she could not shake. What she could not remember was a clear narrative: the weeks blurred into flashes of bodies, dust, and silence. Some moments were excruciatingly vivid—the cologne, the hug, the weight of a child she had to leave—but the rest was blank, and when she tried to explain what happened, her throat closed and the story collapsed. Because those fragments were so potent and the gaps so deep, ordinary things—a kettle boiling, a door closing, the way light fell through curtains—began to feel like echoes of the siege, turning into triggers she couldn't anticipate.

Back in the United States, Leilani returned to her job as a park ranger in a coastal reserve, a position she had loved before. But now the familiar trails felt alien. She became hypervigilant, scanning every hiker for sudden movements, reading threat into a raised hand or a quick step. The hypervigilance itself deepened her sense of threat—she was certain that danger lurked in every unfamiliar bend of the path, so she began avoiding any part of the park she had not already memorized. And that constant sense of threat kept the event alive in her mind, so that on high-alert days the memory surfaced uninvited, as if the adrenaline itself had unlocked it. Once the memory surfaced, even neutral things—a bird's sudden flight, a door slamming—became new triggers, as if the world itself had turned into a series of reminders she could not avoid. Her husband, Derek, noticed she flinched when he came up behind her and that she had stopped going to church, a place that once grounded her. She could not explain why religious spaces felt unbearable; she only knew that the silence there echoed the unbearable quiet of the ruined mosque where she had sheltered. Worse, she refused to see a doctor for a lingering cough, convinced that talking about any part of her body would force her to talk about everything else.

The causal spiral tightened. Each time she smelled a similar cologne—a visitor at the visitor center, a guest at a lodge—the intrusive memory would surge, and with it came a wave of negative appraisals: she had acted against her own deepest values, leaving people behind, failing to save them. Those appraisals made her feel she no longer belonged anywhere, not among her family, not among her fellow rangers, not even among other survivors. The belief that she had failed beyond repair kept pulling her back to the moment of failure, making the memory sharper each time she told herself she was worthless. The thought that her life was not worth living began to surface more often, especially during the long nights when she could not sleep. These appraisals, in turn, amplified her sense of threat: if she was fundamentally flawed, then the world was fundamentally unsafe, and she had to be on guard against everything and everyone. The threat made her avoid even routine medical appointments and religious gatherings—why seek help or solace from a world that had already sentenced her? Once she had come to believe she was beyond redemption, ordinary moments became loaded with danger—a colleague’s casual touch, a stranger’s laughter, even the sight of a parked car could feel like a fresh confirmation that the world was out to expose her. 

Memory gaps played their own cruel role. When she could not tell a coherent story, the fragments—the cologne, the hug, the blank spaces—became her only narrative, and they triggered more intrusive replays. Trying to avoid those replays, she avoided any situation that might evoke them: she stopped attending family gatherings where hugs were expected, and she made excuses to miss staff training held in unfamiliar buildings. But each place she avoided became its own reminder—the long route she took to the visitor center, the pew she no longer sat in, the embrace she turned away from—all of them daily markers of what had happened, turning her own map of safety into a map of the event. Yet avoidance also reinforced her negative appraisals: every time she refused a hug, she told herself she was damaged, unworthy of care. The very strategies she used to protect herself became evidence that she had lost her place in the world.

The maladaptive strategies also fed back into her memory. By refusing to speak about the event, she never constructed a complete story, so the gaps remained, and the vivid moments grew sharper. She began to notice that her hypervigilance—constantly watching for dangerous people—also triggered memories because any sudden movement reminded her of the chaos she could not fully recall. The cycle was self-sustaining: a whiff of cologne led to intrusive memory, which triggered negative appraisals, which intensified hypervigilance, which prompted avoidance, which deepened the memory fragmentation, which made her more vulnerable to the next trigger.

What finally drove Leilani to seek help was an incident in a grocery store. A stranger’s perfume drifted across the aisle, and she froze, then fled, shaking, into a restroom. She stayed there for twenty minutes, certain she was losing her mind. That night, she told Derek that she was tired of being afraid of her own life. She was most afraid that therapy would confirm what she already believed—that she had become someone who did not deserve to feel safe. But she was also, faintly, hoping to find a way back to the person she had been, to the trails she had once walked without scanning for danger, to a world where a hug could still mean comfort.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals cause memory; it only shows memory triggering negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that memory causes triggers; it only shows triggers causing memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not convey that threat causes memory; threat leads to avoidance and hypervigilance but not directly to memory.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that maladaptive strategies cause triggers; strategies like avoidance reduce exposure but do not create new triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
